Retelling: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Over six days He spoke light into darkness, separated sky from sea, filled the land with plants and animals, and set the sun, moon, and stars in their courses. On the sixth day He formed human beings in His own image, male and female, and gave them stewardship over the world He had made. Then He looked at everything He had made and called it very good, and on the seventh day He rested, blessing it as holy.
Themes: Creation; God's Power; Goodness of Creation
Discussion: If God made everything and called it good, then your life has purpose and your body, your work, and your world have dignity. Creation is not an accident, and neither are you. Reflect: 1) What part of creation most reminds you of God's power and goodness? 2) How does knowing you bear God's image change the way you see yourself? 3) How does it change the way you treat others?

Retelling: Daniel was an exile who rose to the top of the Persian empire because of his integrity, and jealous officials plotted against the one thing they could attack: his prayer life. They tricked King Darius into signing a law that for thirty days no one could pray to anyone but the king, on pain of the lions' den. Daniel went home, opened his windows toward Jerusalem, and prayed three times a day just as he always had. Thrown to the lions, he spent the night unharmed — God shut the lions' mouths — and at dawn the king found him alive and threw his accusers in instead.
Discussion: Daniel's courage was built in private before it was tested in public: he did not start praying when the law passed; he simply kept praying as he always had. Faithfulness in small, unseen habits prepares you for the lions' den. Reflect: 1) What private habit of faith sustains you? 2) Where does pressure tempt you to hide your faith? 3) How does Daniel's calm trust challenge your anxiety?

Retelling: For forty days the Philistine giant Goliath — nearly ten feet tall, armored head to toe — taunted Israel's army, and no one dared to face him. David, a shepherd boy sent to bring his brothers food, heard the taunts and asked why no one trusted God to fight. King Saul offered his armor, but David refused it and walked into the valley with only his sling and five smooth stones. With one stone he struck Goliath down, and Israel routed the Philistines. David's victory came not from size or weapons but from faith in the God who had delivered him from lions and bears.
Themes: Courage; Faith; God Fights for Us
Discussion: David did not win because he was brave; he was brave because he knew who God was. The giants in your life are not fought with someone else's armor but with trust in God's past faithfulness. Reflect: 1) What giant is taunting you right now? 2) How has God delivered you before, and how does that fuel courage now? 3) Whose armor are you tempted to wear instead of trusting God?

Retelling: Israel had turned to Baal under King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, and Elijah — God's lone prophet — challenged the 450 prophets of Baal to a contest on Mount Carmel. Each side would build an altar and call on their god to send fire; the god who answered would be the true God. Baal's prophets shouted and cut themselves from morning until evening with no answer. Then Elijah rebuilt the Lord's altar, soaked it with water three times, and prayed a simple prayer — and fire fell from heaven, consuming the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, and even the water. The people fell on their faces crying, 'The Lord — He is God!'
Discussion: Elijah's prayer was short and plain, and God answered with fire — because the issue was never the prophet's eloquence but God's reality. False gods always demand more and deliver nothing; the true God acts. Reflect: 1) What false gods demand your time, money, or devotion? 2) How does Elijah's simple prayer encourage your own prayer life? 3) Where do you need God to show Himself as the true God?

Retelling: Esther was a Jewish orphan who became queen of Persia without anyone knowing her people. When the royal official Haman plotted to destroy all the Jews in the empire, Esther's cousin Mordecai urged her to speak to the king — though approaching him uninvited could mean death. Esther asked her people to fast for three days, then risked her life, saying, 'If I perish, I perish.' She exposed Haman's plot at a banquet, the king had Haman hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai, and the Jews were saved. God's name never appears in the book, but His providence is on every page.
Discussion: Esther reminds us that God works through ordinary people in their ordinary positions — and that courage often means risking comfort for others. You may be exactly where you are 'for such a time as this.' Reflect: 1) Where has God placed you that you might be underestimating? 2) What would courage cost you right now? 3) How do you see God's hidden hand in your life, even when He seems silent?

Retelling: God told Jonah to preach to Nineveh, the brutal capital of Assyria, and Jonah ran the other way — boarding a ship to the far end of the world. God sent a storm, the sailors threw Jonah overboard, and a great fish swallowed him. Three days in the belly of the fish, Jonah prayed, and the fish vomited him onto dry land. He went to Nineveh and preached the shortest sermon in the Bible — 'Forty more days and Nineveh will be overthrown' — and the whole city, from king to cattle, repented in sackcloth. God relented, and Jonah was furious: he had wanted judgment for his enemies, but God wanted mercy.
Discussion: Jonah is the prophet who hated his own message succeeding. God's mercy is wider than our comfort — it extends even to people we consider enemies. Reflect: 1) Who are you tempted to believe is beyond God's mercy? 2) What are you running from that God has asked you to do? 3) How does Jonah's story confront your own desire for judgment over grace?

Retelling: Joseph was his father Jacob's favorite son, and his brothers hated him for it — for his coat of many colors and for his dreams of ruling over them. They sold him to traders bound for Egypt, told their father he was dead, and Joseph spent years as a slave and a prisoner, forgotten by everyone except God. But God raised him up to interpret Pharaoh's dreams and govern Egypt through seven years of famine, and when his brothers came begging for grain, Joseph wept and forgave them, saying, 'You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good.'
Discussion: Joseph's life is the long proof that God works through betrayal, delay, and injustice without ever endorsing them. Forgiveness is not pretending the harm did not happen; it is trusting God's larger purpose while releasing revenge. Reflect: 1) Who do you need to forgive, and what makes that hard? 2) How has God used a painful season in your life for good? 3) Where do you need to trust God's providence when you cannot see the ending?

Retelling: The world had grown so violent and corrupt that God grieved over what He had made. But Noah found favor with God, and God told him to build an enormous ark, even though there was no sea in sight. Noah obeyed, gathering his family and pairs of every kind of animal, and when the rains came the waters covered the earth for forty days and nights. Months later the ark rested on dry ground, Noah sent out a dove that returned with an olive leaf, and God set a rainbow in the sky as the sign of His promise never again to flood the whole earth.
Discussion: Noah obeyed for years before he saw a single drop of rain. Faith often means building the ark before the flood — doing the right thing because God said so, not because the results are visible yet. Reflect: 1) What is one thing God has asked you to do that you have been delaying? 2) How does the rainbow remind you of God's faithfulness after judgment? 3) What does Noah's story teach about God's patience with a broken world?

Retelling: Fifty days after the resurrection, the disciples were gathered in Jerusalem when suddenly a sound like a rushing wind filled the house and tongues of fire rested on each of them. Filled with the Holy Spirit, they began speaking in languages they had never learned, declaring the wonders of God to Jews from every nation who were in the city for the Passover feast. Peter stood and preached that Jesus, crucified and risen, was Lord and Christ, and the crowd was cut to the heart. Three thousand people were baptized that day, and the church was born.
Discussion: Pentecost reverses Babel: where pride scattered the nations, the Spirit gathers them into one people. The same Spirit who made fishermen bold lives in every believer. Reflect: 1) How does the Holy Spirit's power differ from mere enthusiasm? 2) What would Spirit-filled boldness look like in your life this week? 3) How does Pentecost shape your view of the global church?

Retelling: In the days of the judges, famine drove Naomi and her family to Moab, where her sons married Moabite women — and then Naomi lost her husband and both sons. Broken and bitter, she told her daughters-in-law to return to their own people, but Ruth clung to her and said, 'Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God.' Ruth gleaned in the fields of Boaz to keep them alive, Boaz redeemed the family land and married Ruth, and their great-grandson was David, king of Israel — through whom Jesus would come.
Discussion: Ruth's story is small and quiet — no battles, no miracles, just loyalty, hard work, and kindness — and God weaves it into the lineage of the Messiah. Faithfulness in ordinary life is never wasted. Reflect: 1) Who has shown you Ruth-like loyalty? 2) How has God provided for you through ordinary people? 3) What does Ruth teach about belonging to God's people?

Retelling: Samson was set apart from birth as a Nazirite, gifted with supernatural strength to begin delivering Israel from the Philistines. He tore a lion apart, killed a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone, and carried off the gates of Gaza — but he toyed with his calling, and with Delilah he toyed with his secret. Three times she asked where his strength lay and three times he lied, until at last he told her the truth: his uncut hair was the sign of his vow. While he slept she cut it, the Philistines seized and blinded him, but in his final act — praying for strength one last time — Samson brought down the temple of Dagon on his captors and himself.
Discussion: Samson's strength was never really his; it was God's gift, and he treated it as a toy until it was gone. Yet even after failure, God heard his final prayer. No one is beyond the reach of repentance. Reflect: 1) What gift or calling are you toying with? 2) Where does small compromise lead in your life? 3) How does Samson's ending give hope to someone who has failed badly?

Retelling: John the Baptist was preaching repentance at the Jordan River when Jesus came from Galilee to be baptized by him. John protested — he needed Jesus to baptize him, not the other way around — but Jesus said it was fitting to fulfill all righteousness. As Jesus came up from the water, the heavens opened, the Spirit of God descended like a dove and rested on Him, and a voice from heaven declared, 'This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.' The Trinity appeared together at the river, and Jesus' public ministry began.
Discussion: Before Jesus did a single miracle, the Father declared who He was: beloved Son. Your identity is not earned by performance; in Christ, it is declared before you do anything. Reflect: 1) How does Jesus' baptism shape your understanding of your own baptism? 2) What does the Father's declaration over Jesus say about your identity in Him? 3) How does obedience open the door to ministry?

Retelling: God tested Abraham by asking him to take his beloved son Isaac — the son of the promise — up Mount Moriah and offer him as a sacrifice. Abraham rose early, gathered wood, and walked with his son for three days, answering Isaac's question about the lamb with the words, 'God Himself will provide.' At the very last moment, as Abraham raised the knife, the angel of the Lord stopped him, and Abraham saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket. He offered the ram instead and named the place 'The Lord Will Provide.'
Discussion: This is one of the hardest stories in Scripture, and it only makes sense in light of what God did later: He did not spare His own Son. Abraham's trust teaches us that God can be trusted with what we love most — even when we cannot see how. Reflect: 1) What is hardest for you to entrust to God? 2) How does God's provision of the ram point to Jesus? 3) What does it mean to worship God when you do not understand His command?

Retelling: When the time had fully come, God sent His Son into the world — not to a palace but to a stable. Mary and Joseph traveled to Bethlehem for a census, and there, with no room in the inn, Mary laid her firstborn in a manger. That night angels filled the sky over shepherds in the fields, announcing good news of great joy: a Savior had been born. The shepherds hurried to see Him, wise men from the east followed a star bearing gifts, and Mary treasured all these things in her heart. The eternal Word had become flesh and dwelt among us.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Mary; Joseph; The Shepherds; The Wise Men
Discussion: God did not save us from a distance; He entered our world in the most humble way possible. The manger means God meets you in low places, not only in high ones. Reflect: 1) How does Jesus' humble birth reshape your idea of power? 2) Why did God announce the birth to shepherds first? 3) What does it mean that the Word became flesh for you personally?

Retelling: Moses was eighty years old, tending sheep in the wilderness, a fugitive who had failed as a prince and settled for obscurity. Then he saw a bush burning without being consumed, and when he turned aside to look, God called his name and told him to take off his sandals, for he stood on holy ground. God had seen His people's suffering in Egypt and was sending Moses — stammering, reluctant Moses — to lead them out. Moses offered every excuse he could think of, and God answered each one, giving him a brother to speak for him and signs to prove he was sent.
Discussion: God calls the unlikely, the reluctant, and the past-their-prime — and His answer to 'I can't' is 'I will be with you.' Your excuses are not news to God, and they are not disqualifiers. Reflect: 1) What excuse do you most often give God? 2) How does God's name — 'I AM' — speak to your situation? 3) What would change if you believed God's presence, not your ability, is what qualifies you?

Retelling: God spoke to Abram in a land far from home and told him to leave his country, his people, and his father's household and go to a land God would show him. God promised to make him a great nation, to bless him, and to bless all the families of the earth through him. Abram was seventy-five years old, with no child and no map, but he went — taking Sarai, his nephew Lot, and everything he owned. He journeyed to Canaan, built altars to the Lord wherever he camped, and walked by faith in a promise he would not see fulfilled in his lifetime.
Discussion: Abraham's story begins with a call to leave the familiar before he knew the destination. Faith is not certainty about the road; it is trust in the One who calls. Reflect: 1) What 'familiar' thing might God be asking you to leave behind? 2) How do you trust a promise you cannot yet see fulfilled? 3) How does Abraham's story point forward to blessing for all nations?

Retelling: Saul of Tarsus was the church's fiercest enemy — a Pharisee who approved Stephen's stoning and hunted Christians with arrest warrants. On the road to Damascus, a light from heaven brighter than the sun knocked him to the ground, and the risen Jesus spoke: 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?' Blinded, Saul was led into the city, where the disciple Ananias — who feared him — laid hands on him at the Lord's command. Scales fell from his eyes, he was baptized, and within days the man who came to destroy the church was preaching that Jesus is the Son of God. The persecutor had become an apostle.
Discussion: Paul's conversion proves that no one is too far gone — not the zealous opponent, not the person who has done the worst. Grace does not improve the old life; it raises a new one. Reflect: 1) Who in your life seems 'too far gone,' and how does Paul challenge that? 2) How has Christ transformed you, and where is He still transforming you? 3) What does Ananias' obedience teach about welcoming unlikely converts?

Retelling: After a night of trials, Jesus was flogged, mocked with a crown of thorns, and led outside Jerusalem to a hill called Golgotha. There He was nailed to a cross between two criminals, with a sign above His head reading 'Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.' Darkness covered the land at midday, and at three in the afternoon Jesus cried out and gave up His spirit. The temple curtain tore from top to bottom, the earth shook, and a Roman centurion said, 'Truly this was the Son of God.' Joseph of Arimathea laid His body in a new tomb, and a stone sealed the entrance.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Mary; John; Pilate; Simon of Cyrene
Discussion: The cross is where God's justice and God's love meet: sin is not overlooked, it is borne — by Jesus, in our place. There is no deeper proof of love than this. Reflect: 1) What does it mean that Jesus died 'for you' — not just for the world? 2) How does the cross change the way you view your own guilt and shame? 3) What does the torn curtain mean for your access to God?

Story: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Retelling: After ten plagues broke Pharaoh's grip, Israel left Egypt in the night, protected by the blood of the Passover lamb. But Pharaoh changed his mind and chased them with chariots, and Israel found itself trapped between an army and the sea. Moses stretched out his hand, God drove the sea back with a strong wind, and the people walked through on dry ground with walls of water on either side. When the Egyptians followed, the waters returned, and Miriam led the women in a song of triumph: the Lord had hurled horse and rider into the sea.
Discussion: The Exodus is the Bible's great picture of salvation: people who could not free themselves, rescued entirely by God's power, through water, into freedom. When you feel trapped between an army and a sea, the way forward is God's to open. Reflect: 1) What 'Egypt' do you need deliverance from? 2) How does the Passover lamb help you understand Jesus? 3) What song of deliverance could you sing today?

Retelling: God placed Adam and Eve in a garden of abundance with one boundary: they must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The serpent came with a question that planted doubt — did God really mean what He said? — and promised that eating would make them like God. Eve ate, Adam ate, and in that moment everything broke: shame replaced innocence, blame replaced trust, and humanity was sent from the garden. Yet even in judgment, God promised that the offspring of the woman would one day crush the serpent's head.
Discussion: Temptation rarely arrives as an obvious lie; it arrives as a doubt about God's goodness and a promise that disobedience will make us free. The Fall explains why the world feels broken — and why we cannot fix ourselves. Reflect: 1) What doubts about God's goodness do you wrestle with? 2) Where do you see the pattern of blame and shame in your own life? 3) How does God's first promise of rescue give you hope?

Story: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Retelling: A crowd of five thousand men, plus women and children, had followed Jesus into a remote place, and evening was coming with no food in sight. Philip calculated that even a year's wages could not buy enough bread, but Andrew brought a boy who had five barley loaves and two small fish. Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, and broke them, and the disciples distributed food until everyone had eaten their fill — and then gathered twelve baskets of leftovers. The crowd wanted to make Him king by force, but Jesus withdrew: He had come to give a greater bread, His own life, for the world.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Philip; Andrew; The Boy with Loaves
Discussion: Jesus took a child's small lunch and fed a multitude — and then pointed beyond full stomachs to Himself as the bread of life. What you offer God, however small, is never too small in His hands. Reflect: 1) What 'five loaves' do you have to offer God? 2) Where do you need to trust His provision instead of your calculations? 3) How does this miracle point to Jesus as more than a provider of things?

Retelling: A lawyer asked Jesus, 'Who is my neighbor?' and Jesus told a story. A man traveling from Jerusalem to Jericho was robbed, beaten, and left half dead on the roadside. A priest passed by on the other side. A Levite did the same. Then a Samaritan — a member of a people the lawyer's people despised — stopped, bandaged the man's wounds, set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and paid for his care, promising to cover whatever more was needed. Jesus asked, 'Which of these three was a neighbor to the man?' The lawyer answered, 'The one who had mercy on him.' Jesus said, 'Go and do likewise.'
KeyPeople: The Samaritan; The Wounded Man; The Priest; The Levite
Discussion: The parable refuses to let us define 'neighbor' by tribe, religion, or convenience — the neighbor is the one who shows mercy, even across enemy lines. And it quietly points to Jesus, the true Samaritan who stopped for us when we were left for dead. Reflect: 1) Who is the 'Samaritan' in your life — someone you overlook or avoid? 2) What does mercy cost, and are you willing to pay it? 3) How has Jesus been a neighbor to you?

Retelling: On the night before He died, Jesus gathered His twelve disciples in an upper room in Jerusalem to eat the Passover meal. As they reclined at table, He took bread, blessed and broke it, and said, 'This is my body, given for you; do this in remembrance of me.' Then He took the cup and said, 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.' He told them one of them would betray Him, and though they all protested, Judas left into the night. Then Jesus led them out, singing a hymn, toward the garden of Gethsemane.
Discussion: At the table, Jesus gave His friends a meal to remember Him by — bread and cup that still anchor Christian worship today. Every communion is a return to that upper room and to the cross it anticipated. Reflect: 1) What does it mean to you that Jesus shared this meal knowing betrayal was coming? 2) How does the Lord's Supper strengthen your faith? 3) What does the new covenant promise you personally?

Retelling: A younger son demanded his inheritance early — in effect wishing his father dead — and squandered it all in wild living until a famine left him feeding pigs and longing for their pods. Coming to his senses, he rehearsed a speech of repentance and headed home, expecting at best to be hired as a servant. But while he was still far off, his father saw him, ran to him, embraced him, and threw a feast, saying, 'This son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.' The older brother, who had never left, stood outside angry — and the father went out to him too, pleading, 'All that is mine is yours.'
KeyPeople: The Father; The Younger Son; The Older Son
Discussion: This is the gospel in one story: a Father who runs toward rebels and pleads with the self-righteous alike. Whether you are the younger son or the older brother, the feast is open and the Father is waiting. Reflect: 1) Which brother do you relate to more, and why? 2) What keeps you from 'coming home' to God? 3) How does the Father's welcome change the way you welcome others?

Retelling: On the first day of the week, before dawn, Mary Magdalene and the other women came to the tomb and found the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. Angels announced that Jesus, who was crucified, had risen just as He said. Mary wept in the garden until the risen Jesus called her by name, and she clung to Him in joy. That evening He appeared to His disciples behind locked doors, showed them His hands and His side, and breathed peace over them. Thomas, who had doubted, touched His wounds and cried, 'My Lord and my God!' Death had been defeated, and the story of the world had turned.
Discussion: If the resurrection is true, then death is not the end of any story — not yours, not your loved ones', not the world's. Hope is not wishful thinking; it is anchored in an empty tomb. Reflect: 1) How does the resurrection change the way you face death and loss? 2) Why does it matter that Jesus rose bodily, not just as an idea? 3) What new life is God calling you into today?

Retelling: Jesus went up on a mountainside, sat down as a teacher, and opened His mouth to describe life in the kingdom of God. Blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful, the peacemakers. Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you. Do not store up treasures on earth; seek first the kingdom. Do not judge, do not worry, ask and it will be given. He warned against building on sand and ended by saying that everyone who hears His words and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. The crowds were amazed, because He taught with authority.
Discussion: The Sermon is not a list of rules to earn God's favor; it is a portrait of life under a new King, lived by grace. It is meant to be practiced, not just admired. Reflect: 1) Which teaching in the Sermon most challenges you right now? 2) What would 'seek first the kingdom' look like in your week? 3) Are you building on rock or sand — and how can you tell?

Retelling: Fresh from His baptism, Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, where He fasted forty days and nights. There the tempter came with three offers: turn stones into bread, throw Himself from the temple and let angels catch Him, and bow down in exchange for all the kingdoms of the world. Each time Jesus answered not with argument but with Scripture — 'Man shall not live by bread alone,' 'You shall not put the Lord your God to the test,' 'Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.' The devil left Him, and angels came and ministered to Him. Where Adam fell in a garden of abundance, Jesus stood firm in a desert of hunger.
Discussion: Jesus fought temptation the way you can: with God's Word, wielded precisely, in the moment of weakness. Temptation itself is not sin — even Jesus was tempted — but it must be answered. Reflect: 1) Which of the three temptations — appetite, spectacle, or power — tempts you most? 2) What Scripture do you have ready for your weakest moments? 3) How does Jesus' victory give you hope in your own struggles?

Retelling: Three months after leaving Egypt, Israel camped at Mount Sinai, and God descended on the mountain in thunder, lightning, and a thick cloud. He reminded them that He had carried them out of Egypt on eagles' wings, and then He spoke ten words that would shape His covenant people: no other gods, no idols, honor God's name, keep the Sabbath, honor father and mother, and no murder, adultery, theft, lies, or coveting. The people trembled at the mountain and asked Moses to speak to God for them, and Moses received the commandments written on tablets of stone.
Discussion: The commandments are not the price of God's love; they are the shape of life for people already rescued. They show us God's character, expose our need, and point us to the One who kept them perfectly. Reflect: 1) Which commandment most convicts you, and why? 2) How does the law as a gift differ from the law as a burden? 3) How does Jesus fulfill the law rather than abolish it?

Retelling: After the flood, humanity shared one language and settled together on a plain in Shinar. There they decided to build a city and a tower reaching to the heavens, so they could make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. God saw their pride and confused their language, so they could no longer understand one another, and the building stopped. The people scattered across the earth, and the unfinished city was called Babel, because there the Lord confused the language of the whole world.
Discussion: Babel is what happens when human ambition tries to reach heaven on its own terms — impressive, united, and entirely God-less. God scatters what pride builds, but He does not abandon the nations; at Pentecost He begins gathering them back. Reflect: 1) Where do you see 'make a name for ourselves' ambition in your own goals? 2) How does God humble proud projects today? 3) What does Babel teach about unity without God?

Retelling: After forty years in the wilderness, Israel stood at the edge of the promised land facing Jericho, a city with walls so thick that houses were built into them. God gave Joshua a battle plan that made no military sense: march around the city once a day for six days, then seven times on the seventh day, with priests blowing trumpets and the people shouting. When they did exactly what God said, the walls fell flat, and Israel took the city. Only Rahab and her family were spared, because she had hidden Israel's spies and believed Israel's God was the true God.
Discussion: Jericho fell to a strategy that looked foolish — because the battle belonged to the Lord, not to Israel's army. Obedience that looks strange is often the very thing God uses. Reflect: 1) What 'strange' obedience might God be asking of you? 2) How does Rahab's story show that no one is beyond God's mercy? 3) Where are you trusting your own strength instead of God's plan?
